title: The Incomprehensible Birth and the One Godhead
english: … will know him?” (Jeremiah 17:9), meaning “no one.” And about the birth above: “And who will tell of his generation? For his life is taken up from the earth” (Isaiah 53:8). In the most mystical way he called the begetting “generation,” his existence “life,” and his being lifted beyond all measure above the earth and surpassing every mind, “is taken up from the earth.”

For he stands boundlessly higher than any time that one might conceive after circling long in thought, incomparably greater than every quantity, in his substance beyond conceiving, and on every side wholly out of sight, encompassing himself and having nothing of himself outside. Before an incomprehensibility so great the multitude of angels gives way, and so does the whole people of the heavenly ranks. All this they proclaim aloud: David in the eighteenth Psalm, “He made darkness his hiding place, and round about him was his tent” (Psalm 18:11); the Song of Habakkuk, “His excellence covered the heavens” (Habakkuk 3:3); and Matthew, “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son” (Matthew 11:27).

For what is born from creation is begotten through the union of one with another; it is not inseparably one with its begetter, nor does it come forth perfect at once and without passion. With the Godhead it is the reverse. Since creation is of this kind, the Author of all that comes to be is the opposite, and not like his own works, but as the blessed Trinity alone knows. For he would not be incomprehensible if he were comprehended, nor a mystery if he were known, nor divine if he could be contained, nor the Maker of all if he were from time, nor uncompounded and without parts if he were of the order of bodies.

When we hear it said of the Father, “From age to age you are” (Psalm 90:2), and “His truth reaches to the clouds” (Psalm 57:10), we do not set limits to him, but believe that he is eternal; for the age is not his contemporary. In the same way we ought to think of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, for we are speaking of the one nature that rules over all, to which these all-honoured hypostases belong.

The same is sung of the Son: “You are the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 102:27; Hebrews 1:12). And if it is no small thing that it is written of the Father, “He who exists before the ages” (Psalm 55:19), no small thing either is what was spoken in prophecy of his Son, that he is “God before the ages” (Psalm 74:12). It is plain that he is beyond conceiving, as will be shown not much later. And just as the Father “has immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16), or rather is himself immortality, so the Son is “eternal life” (1 John 5:20); and that is the same thing.

And just as the Father is called “one God,” so the Son is called Only-begotten, God, Word, and “one Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 8:6). And as James writes of him, “There is one lawgiver and judge, who alone is able to save” (James 4:12), so the Spirit is hymned by Paul, writing to the Corinthians and the Ephesians, as “one” and “the same” (1 Corinthians 12:11; Ephesians 4:4), and as only, so that by this very quasi-number, if one may put it so, these blessed hypostases are shown to bear the oneness, that is, the singleness, of the Father’s Godhead. And if “God and Lord” is true of the Father, it is just as free of falsehood of his Son and of the Spirit.

For, as we have recalled in many places, the older covenant, guarding their equal honour, declared: “The Lord said to my Lord” (Psalm 110:1); and “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Genesis 19:24); and “God made man according to the image of God” (Genesis 1:27); and “Who is God except the Lord, and who is God besides our God?” (Psalm 18:31). And in the new covenant John said what has already been quoted; Thomas said, “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28); and Paul, “Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17); and again, “as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18); and “May the Lord grant the household of Onesiphorus to find mercy from the Lord” (2 Timothy 1:16; 2 Timothy 1:18). And Job: “The divine Spirit that made me” (Job 33:4), and “the divine Spirit that is still in my nostrils” (Job 27:3).

It is the same thing for Scripture to say “divine” or “God,” as they teach: Paul, writing to the Romans, “his eternal power and Godhead” (Romans 1:20); the Acts, “We ought not to think that the divine is like gold or silver or stone, an image carved by art and human thought” (Acts 17:29); and Peter in his second letter, “that through these you may become sharers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4).

And just as the Father is incomprehensible, so too, according to Paul, the riches of Christ are beyond tracing. For he says, “To me, the very least of all people, this grace was given, to preach among the nations the untraceable riches of Christ” (Ephesians 3:8). And more: “Of his greatness there is no end” (Psalm 145:3), nor “of understanding any number” (Psalm 147:5), as David says, nor “of peace any bound” (Isaiah 9:7), as Isaiah says …

title: The Unoriginate Hypostases
english: “And your incorruptible spirit,” he says, “is in all things” (Wisdom of Solomon 12:1), and “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom of Solomon 1:7). For no one would be found so dull and slow of mind as not to see, from these unfeigned and pure testimonies, the boundlessness of the Only-begotten and of the all-holy Spirit.

And I say that what the Apostle wrote about both hypostases is of equal weight and in like words: what he says of the Father, “God, who is over all and through all and in all” (Ephesians 4:6), and “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever, knows that I do not lie” (2 Corinthians 11:31); and what he wrote to the Romans of the Son, “who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Romans 9:5). Besides this there is also “the fullness of him who fills all in all” (Ephesians 1:23).

Again, what is declared of the Father is alike, “that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28), and of his Son, “where there is neither Greek nor Jew, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free, but Christ is all in all” (Colossians 3:11); and elsewhere, “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven and things on earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is one Lord” (Philippians 2:10-11).

As for the Spirit, both by what was said of him just now and because all that the Father is must be understood of him too, as his Spirit, except for being Father. For he images God both in this and in all things, as it declares: “By this we know that he is in us, from his Spirit, which he has given us” (1 John 3:24).

And of equal force with what was sung of God the Father, “You alone are Most High over all the earth” (Psalm 83:18), is what was spoken in prophecy of the Son in the eighty-seventh Psalm, “Mother Zion will say: A man, and a man was born in it, and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm 87:5), and what was said of the Holy Spirit in the Gospel, “You will receive power from on high when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:8).

And just as the Father is great, among other things, because he knows the Son, so the Son too is great because he knows the Father; and likewise the Holy Spirit, for it says, “So too no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11). And no different from what Paul wrote to the Hebrews about the Father, “For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things” (Hebrews 2:10), is what was spoken in prophecy about the Son, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3), and about the Spirit, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6).

So these glorious hypostases, honoured equally with God the Father, as having received for their portion his divine nature, which is over all, unmixed and beyond compare: how could they be counted among all things under God, as those who vote them creatures would have it?

For just as it is impossible that the Father should not be Father without beginning and in truth (for he did not get this name in time, nor as an added title), so it is impossible that the Son, the Word, and his Spirit should not be without beginning and by nature from his hypostasis. For at once with his being Father (let me be pardoned for putting it so), without any interval the one was begotten and the other proceeded.

So he has not been deprived of being Father of the Only-begotten and of having his Spirit proceeding from him. And because he is Father, he does not differ from the Son and his Spirit either in time or in substance. For if he had begotten later, he would have been changed or altered, which is foreign to the Godhead; and besides, God would be found at some time not called Father, or not being Father, as not yet having begotten.

And the Apostle, setting before the Hebrews how the generation of the Son of God is without beginning and beyond comprehension, writes of Melchizedek: “Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, made like the Son of God” (Hebrews 7:3).

He had been made like him (in that he was not given a genealogy, as it was the custom to do in the tribes of Israel for those held in honour among them) because he is a type and a kind of outline of the Lord, who above is without mother and without time, and below is without father and in time.

And yet Melchizedek was a notable priest, so that Abraham was blessed by him and gave him tithes of the spoils, as the same Apostle says: “Consider how great this man is, to whom Abraham gave a tenth of everything” (Hebrews 7:4). title: In the Beginning Was the Word: The Son Before the Ages and Maker of All
english: … tithing for the Lord comes, is meant in a general sense: “when Melchizedek met him” (Hebrews 7:10), that is, met Abraham.

What, then, is the aim of their empty talk, and where does its absurdity lie? Consider: all who wish to speak of a beginning for him confess an end as well; and by declaring that he came into being, they also accept the death that follows from coming into being. And by supposing that he came to be from things that are not, or from a substance unlike the divine one, they declare him at once mortal and a stranger to the Godhead he shares with the Father. Even to say this, let alone to believe it, is full of every kind of godlessness.

But what are their supposedly strong arguments against “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1)? “The word ‘was’,” he says, “was written of creation too. For Scripture has, ‘In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth; and the earth was invisible and unformed’ (Genesis 1:1-2), and ‘There was a man from Armathaim Sipha’ (1 Samuel 1:1).”

But “In the beginning was” has nothing in common with “In the beginning he made,” any more than the Creator has with the creature. For “was,” in the case of creation, is said and believed only of time, which flows and comes to an end. Creation “was” after it came to be from things that are not. Scripture first said that God made it, and only then added “was,” so that it would not be thought to have come about of itself. But in the case of God the Word, “was” signifies what is beyond all beginning. For “In the beginning,” it says, “was,” and “was God” (John 1:1); and “In the beginning was” drives out “from things that are not.”

That the Son is before the ages and the Maker of the ages, the witnesses testify thus. Paul, writing to the Hebrews: “In many parts and in many ways God spoke of old to the fathers in the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages” (Hebrews 1:1-2). So he inherits what is his own, both as its Maker and as true Son; and he was appointed heir as having become man. And to the Corinthians, in the first letter: “For no one can lay a foundation other than the one that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11); that is, it is impossible to conceive a beginning of the Son. For “in him and through him” (Colossians 1:16) is every beginning.

And David in the seventy-fourth Psalm, singing of the one without beginning: “But God, our King before the ages, worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 74:12). He means Golgotha, calling it the most central place and, as it were, the centre of the land under heaven. There the Son worked salvation for us in his becoming man: by his divine foreknowledge before the age, and in deed when he, the impassible one, suffered for us out of goodness, as he knew and willed, and came, so to speak, even to “the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40). So Ezekiel too prophesies: “Jerusalem herself, I have set her in the midst of the nations” (Ezekiel 5:5).

And in the hundred and nineteenth Psalm: “For ever, Lord, your word endures in heaven” (Psalm 119:89). And the Master himself, speaking of himself, surely shutting the door on heretics, said: “Truly, truly, I say to you, before” the ages came to be, “I am” (John 8:58).

As for his being established as the Maker of all things, bodiless and bodily, not an assistant or a go-between, and at the same time without beginning: besides the testimonies already set out, David also sings in the hundred and fifteenth Psalm, “Our God in heaven and on earth has done all things whatever he willed” (Psalm 115:3). He did not say “whatever he was assigned.” Who then would deny that he who works by himself, of his own will, and has all things running together at his bare nod without delay, belongs to the self-governing and all-governing substance of the Monad?

And in the hundred and second Psalm: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you will remain; and all of them will grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 102:25-27), meaning, “You are without beginning and without end.”

Paul too writes the same, to the Ephesians, “in God who created all things” (Ephesians 3:9), and to the Colossians, “For in him all things were created, in the heavens and on the earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or authorities; all things were created through him and for him, and he is before all things, and in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:16-17). For above him who images God in his very being and is before all things in Godhead no one is set and no one is older, just as below the one who comes after all no one is set and no one is later.

Put another way: if he is before all things, alone from the Alone and in a manner his alone, he was begotten ineffably before every activity and is the Son of the Father in his very being. For it is necessary …
